utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Cvijetic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan and Slobodan Zecevic appearing for Stanisic Defence today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence although he's not present in the courtroom, Igor Pantelic. And welcome back, Judge Harhoff, to our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When we adjourned yesterday evening, I indicated that we would give some thought over night to the last objection which Ms. Korner for the Prosecution formally made, and before we proceed with the witness, as promised, I will attempt to articulate what the -- what our view is on that objection. During the course of yesterday's proceedings from the several versions of that objection because Ms. Korner's last objection was the last expression of a series of objections that she had been taking to the -- certain questions which Mr. Cvijetic was putting to the witness Djeric in cross-examination in terms of the relevance and of course admissibility of certain documentation, which he was putting to the witness on which he was seeking the witness's comment. And from the comments that I myself would have made, it would have been apparent that I found some sympathy with the objections raised by Ms. Korner without formally ruling on the matter and the comments that I would have made would have been to telegraph to Mr. Cvijetic how he should proceed in this matter. On reflection, I think that the -- that the -- we would formally overrule the objection as articulated because notwithstanding, as I've indicated earlier, that -- and this is probably because, like Ms. Korner, I come from a background of a system whereby the way evidence and whatnot is approached may be somewhat different from that of Mr. Cvijetic, and more particularly from the Tribunal which, as has been stated before, on more than one occasion the course of these hearings, the Tribunal of course has its own -- has evolved its own system, which is neither common law nor civil law. But the thrust of Mr. Cvijetic's explanation, as I understand it, is that he is attempting to suggest to the witness and seek his comments, that is the witness's comments, on a view of events which is contrary to what the Prosecution is maintaining, mainly that throughout the witness's relationship with the accused Stanisic, that the witness was, to use a common expression, out of the loop, as it were. And as Mr. Cvijetic has explained, that the case that he is attempting to put is that the witness Djeric was not as disconnected as the Prosecution in its case is seeking to make out. And to that extent, it is our view that he should be permitted to put that -- to put that case by way of suggestion to the witness. The caution, of course, that we would give to counsel for the Defence is that the rules at the end of the day in terms of the admissibility and based on relevance of these documents would apply. So it is -- in putting that case, he should bear in mind that no purpose would be served by seeking to build that on the basis of documents which would not be admissible in any event. The -- I trust that the -- my attempts at an explanation as to why we would permit Mr. Cvijetic to proceed in the manner that he is proceeding towards his conclusion as his time is running out is clear. Thank you. We'll have the witness back in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in. Can I just make it clear, I don't suggest that any of the documents that are shown will be inadmissible at some stage or another, indeed some are already in. What I should make absolutely clear is my objection is the way that they were being put to this witness and the fact that counsel is effectively giving evidence himself and that's the real gravamen of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric, I remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one technical problem that we need to clarify. The binder that I gave to Mr. Djeric, I don't have it. It's been left somewhere here. Is that it? Okay. Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, we can start with document, you have it in your binder under 49, and for the courtroom this is Exhibit 65 ter 932. All right. We have it in both versions. Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the minutes from the 25th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And do you see that among others you also attended that, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since you did attend --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we please now go down in the BH version to the bottom of the minutes, the bottom of the minutes, first page, paragraph 6 from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, in the Serbian version it begins at the end of the page. All right. And it says there that special attention was given to questions of [indiscernible] and ensuring a better information system and it was concluded that in future all visitors to the existing and registered prison must give notice of their visits formally and in time and so on. Do you perhaps remember the agenda and this item on the agenda that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. I remember it well. The matters that had to do with this flower.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you read the passage that has to do with the international Red Cross. All right, you can comment on it now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this agenda and what was discussed was the supply of electricity, and it was said that there were problems and we said that it was not permissible to manipulate and blackmail anyone in terms of the electricity. But we also had problems with electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, what I'm interested is only if you remember with anything with these announced visits. Do you remember if anybody was denied a visit because they did not announce that in advance? Just slowly, just slowly. You must make a break because the interpreters cannot keep up. So do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the particulars. I don't remember. It's possible that there was some problems in relation to that matter, so it was placed on the agenda, but I don't remember, and I know that what was agreed was to open the place up to visits, that nobody could forbid visits, and in that regard from what I can recall certain ministers were charged with keeping an eye on this more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll stop there. I'm going to try to remind you that from the command of the Krajina Corps command refused an application for a visit by Mr. Mazovjtski. Do you remember that case, only because he did not announce his visit in advance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mazovjtski was a high-ranking diplomat. I remember him, and I remember the time that he was performing these duties, and I think that there was some problems between Mazovjtski and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. This is what I wanted know in this part so you know about that problem because it was noted, if you remember, that he did come to a private visit after all, not an official visit and that is why the army stopped him or did not permit him to visit. Do you have anything else to say about that, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I don't know whether it was a private or an official visit. I think -- I don't know. I don't know, but I do know that he was there and that there was some problems with this corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, we will now just go back to the part that has to do with the international Red Cross. It was announced that the representatives of the international Red Cross should be permitted to enter the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We are going to finish with this document. And in the context of this conclusion by the Presidency, I would like now to show you document 1D12. It's already an exhibit. I apologise. In your binder that is number 50. I always forget to tell you that. Yes. Can you please look at the document and then when you are finished, I'm going to ask you. Have you looked at it a little bit? All right. Do you agree with me that this is the practical implementation of the conclusion by the Presidency because the command of the 1st Krajina Corps permitted the entrance of journalists and international representatives, so the position of the Presidency was complied with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this camp was a military camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military at the time was in charge of these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Djeric, I have finished my questions on this topic. And I think I still have to cover one topic from this block. I think that we did not deal with the issue of paramilitary formations. In your testimony in the Krajisnik case you mentioned that problem, and I do have the minutes from the Presidency of Republika Srpska when it was dealing with this matter. I think the government also dealt with the problem.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government did not deal with this problem because this was not in our domain of work. And I did not deal with that matter. I didn't make any agreements or contract any paramilitary formations. I did not finances them --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment, can you please wait, wait. I think that Judge Harhoff at one point told you that you are not accused in this case. Just one moment, please, be patient, be patient. Please be patient, just wait. Be patient. May I be allowed to speak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you and you are answering question. Judge Harhoff told you that you're not supposed to feel like that and there's no need to defend yourself from my questions. I didn't say that you armed them, that you invited them, summoned them. You have to wait for my question, please wait for my question. Now, are we clear on that? In your testimony in the Krajisnik case you mentioned the existence of a major paramilitary formation, the Yellow Wasps and you said that you knew of their existence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of them, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since you attended the sessions do you know whether the Presidency dealt with the matter of paramilitary formations? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was referred to. It was a problem with the president and the military. The army had problems with these paramilitary formations, particularly on the border with Serbia. I do remember that. You are asking me, I cannot really specifically tell you in what sense, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You will agree with me then that the Presidency would be able to receive information about the existence of paramilitary formations from the military organs along that particular line of professional chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could have received information along the civilian line as well, because the paramilitary formations were part of the extra military order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Djeric, what do you mean by the extra military order? What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, I mean, since we are talking about intelligence work, I'm not really well versed in that, but if the paramilitary formations were in a conflict of interest with the interests of the military and their military life and so on, then the Presidency could have been informed about it along the military line, but paramilitary formations are something that -- how can I put it, are outside of the institutions. These are not regulated, regular military formations, so they could have created problems outside of the military sector. How can I put it, outside of their range of activities or where they were positioned, for example, around the borders, around the transports, convoys. So they created certain problems in that respect so that information could have arrived also in another way, not only via the military structures. This is what I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, at some point, you may do it now or later, but at some point you have to tell us how it was with these paramilitary structures and what the problems were. You need not do it now and I will give the floor back to Counsel Cvijetic, but I need you to tell the Court at one point just what the problems were with these military -- paramilitary formations and how you dealt with it. But in order not to waste the counsel's time, I will give the floor back to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for this 65 ter document 192 to be put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I don't want to owe an answer to His Honour, so I am prepared to reply about the paramilitary formations right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask you, I will ask you, but let us look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a report. It says "Army Main Staff." And it's a report on the paramilitary formations in the territory of Republika Srpska. Do you see that, that it's at the heading of the document? This is your document 53, I apologise. Are you able to find it, 53? Have you found it? All right. On the first page, the military intelligence service provides a kind of characteristic of the paramilitary formations, what are their names, the motives, and so on and so forth, and it says the motive for the vast majority of the paramilitaries is looting and committing murders and all sorts of things and so on and so forth. The reason why I wanted to open this document is on page 3 -- we are going to find this in the English version, what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 3 in the Serbian version. And also page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm interested in this statistical data present. In passage 2, in paragraph 2, which is, I think at the very beginning of the English version. Let me just see where the statistical part is. It says that there are about 60 paramilitary units which were registered between 4- and 5.000 people in total, and the ones they consider to be the most important are listed here. In the area of Zvornik these are the Yellow Wasps, 170 men, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next large group that the army paid attention to is mentioned on page 5 of the Serbian version, and in the English version it's the second paragraph on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your version it's the fourth or fifth paragraph, do you see? Rather large group has been registered on the territory of Teslic municipality. By showing you this, I simply wanted to let you know what kind of units these were and what their strength was. And as you yourself said that you knew about these Yellow Wasps. Through the next several documents I will show -- I will deal with the question of how these two units ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now have 1D00-5403. Just let me see. And open page 8 in the BH version. It's page 9 in English. Could you scroll down a little bit, please. And page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is just the beginning, we'll have to scroll down slowly on these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a criminal report concerning the arrest and prosecution of this large Teslic unit by the Banja Luka public security service, the Teslic public security station, and I want to show the witness what number of persons were arrested, and we can see that right away. And there is a description of the crimes they are charged with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for your assistance it's the Mice. It's the Mice group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to ask the witness whether he knew if these were the Mice but all right now you've said it. In the English version can you scroll down so that the other names can be seen. Only the first accused is written on this part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I don't know what document this is, I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document 54. I do apologise, I -- again I forgot to tell you what number it is in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So look at page 8 now that you've found it. You'll come to the criminal report if you look through the document. There is it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in English could we scroll down, please. Yes, yes. And just keep scrolling down, keep scrolling down, please, so that you can see how many men were arrested and how many witnesses and victims were interviewed. Yes, and please just keep going in the English version. So, yes. So let's go on to the next page and then the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If you look at the list of exhibits, you'll find there are 160.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While that's happening can I correct the LiveNote, it's page 13 line 21 where I speak, Mice is M-i-c-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we have to go to page 82 in the English and 54 in B/C/S, so we have the page in English. Yes, now we have it in B/C/S as well. And now please scroll down in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found 54, page 54, Professor? The heading is "Report." You can see it on the screen. This is a list of witness statements made by witnesses of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt this again but this is now becoming a speech. There is going to be a multitude of witnesses who can deal and who are going to deal with this particular group and what happened in Teslic. It was a slightly unique situation. Now, before we go on with this exercise, I think -- I do really think that Mr. Djeric should be asked whether he knows anything about the circumstances of this group or this incident, and if he doesn't, this should be an end of it. It's not that we are trying to stop this evidence going in, it will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you what the purpose of this exercise is. As the witness is evaluating the work of the Ministry of the Interior, I wish to show him the scope and the scale of actions undertaken by the ministry in order to eliminate paramilitary formations. So I'm not going to comment on the content of the document with the witness since evidently he is not in a position to discuss it, but I just want to demonstrate that in order to deal with a case of this kind, what it takes to open an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, did you know about the activities of the Ministry of the Interior to eliminate such groups?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Work was done on that but as regards this group specifically, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the attempts to eliminate the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that something was done because the Yellow Wasps were active in the area towards Serbia, around the river Drina, and there were frequent problems with that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of the Interior in cooperation with the military police eliminated this large group also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is a type of question that Ms. Korner -- to which Ms. Korner was objecting. That last one was not a proper question, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness knows the facts, Your Honour. He knows that the group was broken up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, then let the witness give the evidence. Not you. Ask him a question and we will hear his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how these proceedings ended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What proceedings are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Against the Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this group was broken up. I know that. Quite simply there were problems at the border around Zvornik. For instance, I recall that they even pulled a minister out of a car and ordered him to lie down and graze grass. Those Yellow Wasps did that. And that's how I received this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they committed war crimes on the territory of Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information that reached the government had more to do with obstructing traffic, economic activities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Will you believe me if I say that in cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska and the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, persons were prosecuted for war crimes committed on the territory of Zvornik municipality? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't because these are military and paramilitary units that did not belong to me. They belonged to the government and the president, so he dealt with them. So I don't have so much information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was, do you believe me when I say that this is true, or would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything can be proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that you have mentioned the Presidency, you were present so I have to show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 3033. It's 64 in your binder, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's 3033. Have you found it? 64. It's a session of the Presidency. This document refers to a session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska held on the 28th of September 1992, and you were among those attending; am I right? Please take a look.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the first item on the agenda was engagement of volunteers in the defence of Republika Srpska. Do you remember that item of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that these volunteers were engaged because they were sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 1 where it says that all volunteers will be put under the single command of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the principle. They couldn't act on their own initiative of their own free will. They had to be under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It also says that the Presidency stressed that the ban on the establishment and activity of paramilitary units was still in force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to attend the session of the Assembly when this problem was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose I was. What Assembly do you mean? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not an ordinary Assembly. It was the Assembly where your resignation was accepted when the government fell, on the 24th of November 1992. You were present then, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. It's document 65 in your binder, Professor, and it's 65 ter 933. It's 65 ter 933.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version we should be on page 18. And in the English version - let me just find it. It's on page 23 in English, the speech of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read Mrs. Plavsic's contribution to the discussion? Have you found page 18? Please find it. And Mrs. Plavsic's contribution to the discussion begins at the bottom of the page. Well, now you've found it. Please read what Mrs. Plavsic said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to say, I read this part to him when I dealt with it. He has already read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no harm in him reading it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What she says about paramilitaries, that she invited them -- yes, it says Mrs. Plavsic, but as I remember, Madam Prosecutor, it wasn't this speech. It was another one when Mrs. Plavsic was talking about percentages of the territory and so on. It's not this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read the part that I asked you to read. And move on to the next page. Have you had a look? You are talking about paramilitary formations. It's this passage in the middle where she lists them.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is Mrs. Plavsic's reaction to the activities of Mr. Mico Stanisic breaking up these paramilitary formations, and even the term he uses, paramilitary formations that is. So what do you say to this standpoint of Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She often spoke like this. This is her opinion. Of course, I did not agree with it. I never approved such things being done. That's why I should have clarified about these paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people, including her, allowed themselves to go around looking for some sort of paramilitary units and engaging them. I did not approve of this nor did I consider that that was the way things should be done, but there were more people who held such opinions, that these were people fighting for the Serbian people, that they were not criminals and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So her opinion was not something unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that this is Mrs. Plavsic's personal opinion, or the opinion of some other deputy, but what might have concerned your minister who invested so much effort was that this was followed by applause. He was not applauded for eliminating this sort of group. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are people's perceptions. The minister knew that his task was to implement the government policy and the Presidency's policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But such a high-ranking body would be expected to provide its support; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what political life is like, you know. There are always some who are for and some who are against. People see things this way or that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is an extremist opinion, the one held by Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We're finish with this document. You can close the file. I'll just ask you one thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before do you that, can I just ask, you put to the witness that this was Mrs. Plavsic's response to Mico Stanisic breaking up the paramilitary units. Can I just ask where you get that from? In Mico Stanisic's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm drawing this conclusion from Mrs. Plavsic's speech where she says to Stanisic, you call them paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's the objection I have. It's asserted by Mr. Cvijetic giving evidence that this is the reaction to Mico Stanisic breaking up the paramilitaries. There's no such reference in his speech to which Mrs. Plavsic refers. So, as I say, it would be better if speeches were not made and simply questions were put.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you're right. There was a huge polemic at that Assembly between Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Mandic, and Mr. Djeric, and inter alia they discussed the results of the work of the ministry of the interior, the Prosecution of paramilitary formations. That was why this discussion was held and why Mrs. Plavsic reacted. If you read the whole of the minutes, that was the conclusion I reached. The witness may need not agree with me, but her discussion speaks for itself, and it's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you know how many men the administration for the prevention of crime at the Ministry of the Interior had?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you that this administration which was in charge of these large operations -- well, when one says administration, you have the impression that this involves hundreds of inspectors and policemen. Do you know how many were actually employed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How many people were employed in this administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were working under very difficult conditions. The government was being set up in a meadow without the proper infrastructure, without any institutions, without appropriate staff. It was something far removed from any modern understanding of what a ministry or a government should look like. We didn't have large numbers of trained staff, civil servants who were able to deal with that kind of work. But I can't answer your question how many people were employed. I'm sure there were far fewer than the situation required, but we couldn't find people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you that there are no more than five, believe it or not. Can you believe that this was done by only five people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe you. There were ministries that didn't have more than five people working on them because everybody else had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, 20 -- it's been corrected right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, the time and you are not a witness where -- with whom we can show all the things that the ministry did, and I claim that I didn't even show you point 1 per cent of the results of the work of the ministry for the Internal Affairs in persecuting -- in prosecuting the perpetrators of the most serious crimes and sentencing them. Do you agree that the results of the MUP were what I say they were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that the ministry didn't work or that it didn't do a vast amount of work. But I am going to say that I, as the president -- the prime minister, was not satisfied with the engagement of the ministry, or rather the minister, in terms of the implementation of the government policies. I never said that the ministry wasn't working, but it's more of a question of how much more it could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And that is precisely the next topic. We don't need documents. Mr. Djeric, you received the mandate to form the mandate at the Assembly in March 1992, late March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, but since I owe --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, just leave that. I'm the one who is asking. Is it correct that this was in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then at the Assembly session, you received only two ministers, you were given only two ministers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Buha, the minister for foreign affairs and the minister for the interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that - how shall I put it - the consolidation and the staffing of the government lasted until July 1992; is that correct more or less approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was a long period of time, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you said that you submitted your resignation. Now we are going to do a little bit something about the dates. I know you don't like that. Resignation, which you were expecting to be accepted at the Assembly in Prijedor which was held in October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you replied. You would agree with me that perhaps you were mistaken about the dates. You said that this was on the 9th of October, and the Assembly was held on the 31st of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the dates are concerned, believe me, I didn't have the opportunity to check the precise dates. There was manipulation in the newspapers with these dates so that I'm not sure, and that is why I would rather stay with the events so the Prijedor Assembly, when I submitted my resignation and signed it, because I was asked to have it signed, so I signed it, so conditions were created all of them for it to be accepted at that time. But for certain reasons, this was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can I help you about those dates and even I'm not so good with dates. Is there a possibility that on the 9th, you wrote your resignation which should have been placed before the Assembly on the 31st?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of unclear things for me there still and I'm even thinking that perhaps this was in late September, but I cannot simply -- the best way to establish the precise date is to establish the exact time of the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There's a lot of background noise. We are finding it difficult to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I signed the resignation and then in the Zvornik Assembly, this is the only thing that I can state with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you what the reason is. My reason is not the wish to confuse you with the dates. I would like to calculate the effective time from the time that the government was operating in its full composition, so July, August, September. We can take that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You did not conceal your resignation from your ministers, if I'm not mistaken, you submitted it publicly, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it, submitted it, I signed it, and I was actually waiting for the first Assembly session in order to be able to submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat the time for the transcript. This is June, July, August, September, and October. Five months we are talking about. And you will know about the parliamentary principle that each government should be given the famous 100 days to do something in order to be able to evaluate its work. You know about that rule, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Those 100 days in normal circumstances, and 100 days in the conditions that you were working in could not be considered to be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, when we look at the number of the meetings that were held, the agendas, the problems that you managed to solve in that period, the proposed laws and documents and other measures, it has to be said that the government was working despite of all the initial problems that both you and I talked about, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not disputing that it was working and that we are talking about vast tasks and big assignments. A lot of work. Every few days practically we were in session. The government was permanently in session, permanently in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you will agree with me that the successes of the government were actually the successes of the ministries because the government in itself does not exist as a body unless it is comprised of ministries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not disputing that. But the president -- the prime minister, the person that is heading the government also tries to achieve the best possible results.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree also that the problems that the government was encountering, and we are talking about strong local power, the Serbian Autonomous Regions, Crisis Staff, current wartime problems, refugees, crime, that those problems were problems of the ministries as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a context and environment in which the government and its ministries were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, very early on you requested a reconstruction of the government. You said even at the Assembly that you sought that as early as May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I did sense certain problems in the government, in the functional and personnel sense, so I don't know if I did that in May, but -- this is July that we are talking about, August, and so on I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I do have a reference. I do have the minutes of the Assembly when you -- session when you submitted your resignation, and you literally said a long time ago in May, five months ago, I began to talk about this problem in the work of the government.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The path was, first of all, to try to resolve the problems within the government, then we referred to the political leadership and this was then discussed there for several months, and then in the end it had to be brought before the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, who did you talk to about this problem that you were asking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was informed about it. First of all, the ministers knew about it, the government knew about it. They knew that I was asking for a reconstruction of the government primarily in relation to these two ministries: The Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior. Although there were some others as well, other ministries but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking about those two ministries, first of all, so the government, the political leadership, all of them were informed about it and this was constantly debated. We were looking for a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Specifically the question was did you specifically discuss this matter with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You have to say yes -- answer with a yes to my question because we need to move on. We must move on. At that point in time when practically the government was not consolidated, it had not been placed under oath, you had no results but still you were seeking a reconstruction of the government. What was the response of Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His reply was that the ministers were working well, that this should not be done, and so on and so forth. And he stood by these two ministers. That is the main thing that I would like to emphasise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You would agree that in May, you didn't have the results of the work of any of the ministries and that on the basis of the results you were unable to evaluate somebody's work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May, that's something else. I'm not talking about May. I'm talking about this time there, the later period. In May, in May, what was said was discussion in terms of looking for the adequate or appropriate people. It was a question of finding these people at the location where the government was. Finding the right people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the Krajisnik case, you said that you could not influence the composition of the government and that in some way it was imposed on you, you had to take these ministers from before, from the B&H and the ministerial counsel and that you personally were not in a situation to create the composition of the government; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said in the Krajisnik case, and I'm saying that today now. The party was the one that put forward the cadres, not in the sense of providing alternatives. It would always be one single solution, so I was not able to choose in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you more questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who proposed you for that post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The party too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS party. Serbian Democratic Party. It participated in the government and they put me forward for that position. I was on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Just finish that answer. You've answered me and that's that. Who proposed you for the ministerial council of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the party and the presiding of the council of ministers at the time, Mr. Simovic. He made that agreement with the party president and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, you've answered, now let us move on. Who gave you the mandate to form a government, the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which party and which president?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead, say it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian Democratic Party. The Serbian Democratic Party was the one and then on behalf of the party before the Assembly, and this was in Pale in March, I was put forward as a candidate by Biljana Plavsic. From what I understood, she was the one who was heading the party's personnel commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered. Mr. Djeric, in all parliamentary systems when a party wins an election and when it has an absolute majority, it is the one that puts forward the candidate to form the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And if it has a majority, absolute majority, it doesn't have to put forward a coalition partner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it logical that each prime minister designate takes care to secure the support of the Assembly majority when he is putting forward the composition of the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So is it logical that you put forth -- forward such a composition of the government because you were expecting to receive the support of the party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The support is given to me by the party because its deputies are in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I'm talking about. So you are careful to secure support? You do take that into account?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I don't have any choice in that matter. I'm not a party member, but I am on the list of that party, and I receive my cadres from that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to read to you the names of some members of the government about whom you said that you would never have picked them had you been in a position to choose. So Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic, with the explanation that they -- and you said that here in the courtroom as well, were closer to the president than to you. Is that the essence of your objection to the two of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I would never have considered the two of them to be members of the government because of the functioning of the government and functioning in the government, and what you are asking me simply -- well, one needs to have in mind here that simply speaking we at the time had a system --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well -- I apologise but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let him finish, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the cross-examination you have to answer me. Just tell me, well, this is the reason -- if that is the reason why they were closer to the president than to you, this is what you said in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was not the reason, you know. It was not the main reason. They just ignored the government. They ignored the government because they considered themselves to be the president's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. No, no, no, I have to stop him. You replied, you replied to my question but in a different way, but please tell me, what did you find with Mr. Pejic, the deputy prime minister, what about him, why wouldn't you have taken him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he tended to work more for his own benefit than to further the goals of the government, and secondly, Pejic also had health problems. He was an invalid, although he did have the proper professional background. He had been dealing with financial matters for years, but because of his handicap had they asked me, he would never have been nominated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why would you not want Subotic as the minister of defence in your government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was difficult for him to establish communication with the military. It simply did not function as a relationship, or rather, not sufficiently. It could have been done much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm also interested in the fact that you would never have worked with Mr. Trbojevic who was never a party member. What was wrong with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trbojevic was a careerist. He had careerist ambitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What you held against Mr. Kalinic was that he leaned more towards the president?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it is more important to clarify things here, to explain them. We are talking about people, people who had a good understanding of the system as it existed at the time. It was a presidential system. The government was simply an appendage of the president and the Presidency, and they counted on being appointed by the party even if I resigned. They knew what they were doing there, and they were simply gathering around the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have to interrupt you now because my time is running out. The minister of external affairs, Buha, you didn't like him either?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I didn't like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you hold against him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did his job, he did it, but I'm simply bearing in mind the fact that people simply didn't understand the function of the government in a parliamentary democracy. We said something and then they set out to do something else. It's very important to say this. You are talking about a time when I had already handed in my resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just be patient. You mentioned three people: Buha, Pejic, and now Milojevic [phoen] have leanings towards Belgrade, and I would never have taken them, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they all had -- well, people acted in a way, the way I was trying to reconstruct the government to make it more effective and so on. People began to look for ways to turn things to their own advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't like Ostojic either. You said he was an extremist and he was a minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he proved to be an extremist, but you keep mentioning things from the last session that was already at the finish line, because, sir, counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just answer my question, please. I do have to interrupt you. In the case of Ostojic, was this the decisive reason when you said he was an extremist in your view? You said that in the Krajisnik case, I'm just quoting your words.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an extremist, and if I had been able to constitute a new government, he would never have been a member of it because he was an extremist, and that's, I'm just speaking hypothetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the ministerial departments. Ministry of Justice, Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, two deputy prime ministers, the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Defence, all of them were key ministries. So with whom did you achieve the successes we spoke about? For example, did the Minister of Forestry really plant forests in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government did do its job, but it could have done it better. Especially in the case of two ministries, and don't forget one other thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'll move on and mention a specific ministry. Wouldn't it be fair to say that the government achieved its greatest successes in these key areas: Security, defence, and probably justice? I won't mention any more. Wouldn't it be fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not how it was. Those were the two most important, most necessary ministries, and I wanted to achieve more in those areas. That's why I asked for those changes. These were key ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. We then now have to move on to the session when your resignation was adopted. Do you remember what you said at that session of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you are moving on to something new, perhaps we should take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, one brief apology to the professional services. At the beginning of the transcript it says, and I said that there was a technical problem with the binder. Actually, it was my problem. I had forgotten the binder and they had put it away, and so it was not a matter of the problem being a problem of the technical service, but it was my own problem. So I would like to have that corrected in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, we are now finding ourselves at the Assembly where the resignation of the government was being discussed. This is document, if you would like to refresh your memory and open the document, it's document 65 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I have to explain that in English it's probably page 15. First of all, I have to give you the document number. It's 65 ter 933. It will be three pages: 15, 18, 19. Those three pages are relevant, up until page 23. So from page 15 onwards and that's how we will follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I think that in the Serbian version it begins on the 10th page. This is your address. Mr. Djeric, you will agree with me that the Assembly is a body in which all problems are discussed in the most democratic way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That was the opportunity for your ministers -- to tell your ministers that you were not happy with what it is about their work that you were not satisfied with; is that correct? Is that correct, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, I'm asking you. Did you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The question is, did you use the opportunity in the Assembly and tell each of the ministers to their face what you thought was not good about their work directly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tell people at the government sessions what was not good and what they were supposed to change and so on and so forth. I don't want you to misunderstand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I have to stop you. Did you use that at the Assembly at such a place where really decisions are being made on the value of the work of the entire government and each minister individually, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply I did not discuss certain ministers at the Assembly. I mean, you understand ministers are member of the government and you have to understand that the government is a working entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, if you didn't, and I see that you didn't, Mr. Mandic, Momcilo, minister of justice, and Mr. Stanisic are calling you out directly and they are saying -- stating their objections to your work and asking you directly to come out and tell them specifically what in the professional sense as ministers or their ministries you find fault with. Do you remember their addresses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember their addresses, but they know very well this is just a manoeuvre of theirs. They know what my objections were, what the objections of the government were on their account. It wasn't just me as the prime minister, but it was all the other ministers, they all knew very well about the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. A specific question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a session where the resignation of the prime minister was being accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Listen to me now, please don't interrupt me. That is the session of the Assembly, and Mr. Mandic says that you never asked a report from the ministries on their work. Is that correct what Mr. Mandic said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct because the government works by asking for ministries to report back to it and the ministries react with their reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the English says that "has anyone ever seen a report about our work, whose fault is that whether Momcilo Mandic or Djeric? It doesn't say, Mr. Cvijetic, what you've just para-phrased. I think if you are going so put things you've ought to read from the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question specifically, my question is, did you ask for reports on the work on these two key ministries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could I have not asked for them. Yesterday we looked at some of them. How would the reports have arrived had I not requested them? The government works by periodically asking for reports from the ministries about their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. The essence of my question is, yesterday we looked at the reports on the work of the Ministry of the Interior, and I did not hear one single objection in the professional sense about the results of the work of the ministry, and not in the courtroom either. I'm going to of move to the address -- I just apologise for one second. I'm going to move to the discussion of Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Stanisic is remarking that his only -- that your only argument at his expense is that he is allegedly Radovan's man. That's what it says in the report. This is page 16 of the Serbian version and we are going to do our best to find -- oh, yes, here it is. This is page 21 or 22, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And -- page 21 towards the end. And just let me finish my question. Mr. Stanisic says that that is no argument as far as he is concerned, wasn't it then called for you to come out and bring out some other arguments?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that doesn't apply. That is really making the case banal by Mr. Stanisic. He is making light of it. He's trying to find an excuse for himself and to get out of it. I didn't have remarks or objections in terms of his work because he is the president's man, but because he was not implementing to a sufficient degree the policy of the government. It was his problem that he was ignoring the government, that he was constantly spending time with the president. That is his problem. I apologise. Many of these things could have been done by the bureaucracy by the clerks of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, Mr. Djeric, you have responded now to this objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Cvijetic, don't para-phrase. Read the exact words from the transcript and then identify them also please in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version it's page 16 at the bottom, and now we will see, let us see page 21 at the bottom, last paragraph, I'm going to read what it says so that we don't have the case that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "For that reason we insisted that somebody cannot, as they see fit, say you are not good because I feel that you are Radovan's man. As far as I'm concerned, that is no argument." Have I quoted correctly the words? Mr. Djeric, allow me to put the question to you now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So I have summarised the discussions from the Assembly, and I have had some substantial problems to present to you the results of the work of the Ministry of the Interior. I was following your reactions when I was presenting you with this evidence, and I'm listening to you now. I must note that your only argumentation that Mr. Stanisic was Radovan's man and that you have know other objection in the sense -- in terms of his professionality -- professionalism, quality, and the scope of work of such a large ministry that was part of your government; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. I disagree completely. Your questions and your arguments and so on and so forth in the spirit of -- are in the spirit of your client. What I want to say is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, all right, all right, you've responded. I'm satisfied with the answer. Mr. Djeric, Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you cannot interrupt a witness's answer like this because you don't like what he is going to say. He must be allowed to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Korner and Your Honours, the witness has answered my question. I'm running the procedure, I'm putting the questions, and I'm not going to remind Ms. Korner about the way she questions witnesses, and I was never opposed to such a manner. Stop, stop, stop, so I'm telling my witness stop. I received an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you didn't get an answer. I had only just began to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The specific answer was that you disagree with me, and we don't have to agree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wanted to answer you as well. It's not only that I disagree. Your Honours, in the minutes or in the report you have a place where it says -- where it is emphasised that this entire problem was made up by the prime minister and that the prime minister is rebelling against the president of the republic and that is why he is not tolerating these two ministers and so on and so forth. This is not true, this is not true. I knew very well what my position was and what the position of the president of the republic was. Especially during a regime of one party. So this whole story is made up. I exclusively had problems with those two ministers because they did not engage themselves sufficiently on the implementation of the policies of the government. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that you are talking about the president, did you yourself say we have to put to him his testimony in the Krajisnik case because it's been admitted into evidence, did you yourself say that you diverged in concept from the president of the republic, that he wanted a strong presidential system and you were against the government being marginalised; is that where you diverged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was resolved by the constitution. The position of the government and the position of the president. But we had different ideas primarily as regards the effectiveness of government. Because the president, when these two ministries are concerned, in particular said we'll deal with this later, but I wanted things to be dealt with. I wanted prosecutions to take place in compliance with the government decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, what prosecutions did you want to take place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted everything done in compliance with the conclusions of the government. Because as you see we spoke about the security of persons and property, about crime. Crime was the greatest evil in our society at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. When it comes to prosecutions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You will remember the caution, counsel and witness, about allowing a gap so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check whether everything is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before you proceed, I would be grateful if you would be kind enough to explain where you are going with all of this? For a long time we have been dealing with the issue of whether or not this witness was satisfied with your client's work during government time in 1992. And whatever the reason is, as much as I can figure out, this witness was not satisfied with Mr. Stanisic's performance in the government. And allegations have been made, I don't know whether they are substantiated, allegations have been made that apparently there was some rift between the government and the Presidency and Stanisic apparently -- apparently I emphasise was on the side of Karadzic. Now how does this assist your case? That's what I don't understand. This is why I'm asking where you are going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the witness mentioned, prosecutions I intend to put one more document in this line of questioning, and I think it will answer your question. I propose that we ask the witness to leave then I can answer your question. We could discuss arguments and cases when the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not interested in your answer. I'm interested in how this witness can testify and contribute to the finding of the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the direction I'm going in, and I wish to put a document to the witness and ask him to comment on it. Could the witness be shown 65 ter 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's 66, Mr. Djeric, in your binder. The last document in your binder. Mr. Djeric, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic's letter sent to you personally and to the president of the republic personally. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you see the contents of the letter? Take a look. As you see, in this letter, Mr. Stanisic in the first part of the letter as a professional, draws attention to the danger that war crimes might be committed and not prosecuted. He refers to international conventions and claims that you personally have not sufficiently activated yourself in dealing with these matters. Yesterday I showed you Mr. Stanisic's order form from the field, and here on page 2 you see he says regardless of who the perpetrators are and what their ethnicity is. I asked you, Mr. Djeric, yesterday or on Friday, who raised the issue of war crimes in the government, the issue of documenting war crimes, prosecuting war crimes, and you didn't answer my question. You didn't want to answer it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government put this on the agenda at my initiative as the prime minister. I'm the one who was leading the government proposing agendas and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And was this letter -- what prompted you to put this item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this letter is a manoeuvre by Mr. Stanisic after pressure from me to replace these two ministers, in particular Minister Stanisic, so he went on the counter-offensive trying to have me replaced. When they saw that the president was on their side, they went on the offensive against me and that's why he wrote this letter, and I was the one actually who prompted the government to deal with violations of laws and regulations and to prosecute all this. You can see this from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Stanisic did not stop at this letter. I showed you yesterday specific documents dealing with -- discovering the perpetrators of war crimes and prosecuting them. Do you remember when and at what government session you initiated discussion of this issue?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the one proposing the agenda, so it was my initiative that this issue be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, finally, wouldn't it be fair to answer my question by saying that you accepted your minister's initiative in putting this item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. I'm the one who implemented the government policy and its programme and carried out our duties. And it's highly impertinent to say to me that I was the one obstructing this. There are witnesses who can testify to who did what.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, since you often use the term government, the government did this, the government did that, who was the government? Were you the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't me. It was the ministries. It was the organ coordinating the ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic with his minister, was he the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the results of his work on this issue are successes of the government, results of the government, but you cannot take the credit for this yourself without saying that he contributed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not in dispute. But every president, or rather, every prime minister wants to achieve better results. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Mr. Djeric, I finished with these documents. It is my duty to take you through some documents of the government sessions and Assembly sessions and the National Security Council. I'm not duty bound to explain the reasons for this to you, in order to evaluate the possibility for the implementation of certain documents. I think that we owe an explanation to the Bench as to how the Republika Srpska got its president. You didn't answer that question, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What president?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The collective for Presidency and the president. You said that Radovan Karadzic was only a member of a party and that you don't know how he came to perform that duty.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember, that is, when this Presidency was appointed. I remember very well when he was elected at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you were the prime minister, you are a university professor. I expected you to be aware of certain basic things from our constitution and that you will be able to tell the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the constitution of Republika Srpska, that's 65 ter 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, we may have, but can you inform us before we leave this document what is the date of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. 18th of July 1989 [as interpreted] on the last page. It's not on the first page, it's on the last page that the date is mentioned. Yes, the 18th of July, 1992. May I proceed? Could we now have the constitution, please. 65 ter 49. And could we come to the end, the final provisions. 140. Could you scroll down until we come to 140. Article 137. Changes -- amendments, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Article 142, on the monitor. It's on the monitor. I don't think you have this in hard copy. Let's just see it in English. 40. It says: "The Constitution of the Republic may be amended by a constitutional amendment or a constitutional law." Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 28th of February, the Assembly adopted the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would like to have this document shown you, 1D00-4266. In the Serbian version it's further down. It's further down. On the right-hand side there is a column where the law begins. Over -- technically you can now move on to the next page. Article 4. Excellent. And now in the English version, can we have the same article and then we can deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
