utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, please read Articles 4, 5, and 6. These mention the government. In Article 4, the manner of election of the president of the republic is provided for. I wish to jog your memory, and that's in Article 5, item 2: "Until the election of the president of the republic, the function of the president shall be carried out by the members of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not that I don't remember that. I do remember that. Those two members of the Presidency represent the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they performed the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that's how continuity was maintained until the election of the Presidency, the collective Presidency. And now we have this law on amendments to the constitution, and it's in the package, Your Honour, which has not been admitted into evidence yet, so I will just read out the provision which refers to changes in the way the president is elected. This Article 5 that you read out was amended, and now it reads as follows: "Until the election of the president of the republic, the office of president will be carried out by a three-member Presidency elected by the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then the next item is: "The Presidency shall elect the president from the ranks of its members." Mr. Djeric, this amendment to the constitution was adopted on the 12th of May 1992 by the Assembly. Ms. Korner showed you the minutes, and I can show them too, from the Presidency session which you attended on that day when Radovan Karadzic was unanimously elected president of the Presidency. You were there too?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I find it hard to believe that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have left for a moment, but I really don't remember that. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I can't but tell you, you attended the Assembly session presided over by Mr. Krajisnik. When you were shown the minutes, you said they were false, that they were a pure forgery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the Krajisnik case when you testified, I'm not sure whether by Mr. Stewart or by the Prosecutor, but you were shown the minutes from the Presidency session not attended by Mr. Karadzic and Mrs. Plavsic, and you attended it, and you said that this was a forgery pure and simple; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that because I don't remember, I don't remember Krajisnik presiding. That's my argument. It was either these two members who presided or later on it was Radovan. That's what I can remember. Both then and now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Krajisnik case line 15. Judge Orie put this to you. And you said to Judge Orie: "That is a forgery pure and simple."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that Krajisnik presided over the Presidency. I said it then, and I'm saying it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I can't help telling you this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you need then to look at what he said further about this at page 27172 when he was cross-examined about that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I have the next page. This is the only page I've brought with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But can you explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Krajisnik ever, ever presiding over a Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I really am trying to preserve your credibility, but with respect to the government instructions put to you by Judge Orie, I have the page number and everything, you said that's a forgery too. Page 27108, line 18.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The document I put to you first yesterday, government instructions on the work of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to you that I -- there was a document, some sort of instructions, and I sent this document to the Crisis Staffs because of my own responsibility. As I said, I said that I think Karadzic also signed this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The page number was 10718.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic. It's no good partially quoting. He was further asked questions about that at page -- of the Krajisnik transcript page 27163, when he said that he didn't remember. Not that it was a forgery. You must, must make a note of all the references in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness responded, and he explained what he meant when he said that it was completely fabricated, and this is the problem. You don't seem to remember that much, Mr. Djeric. That seems to be the case in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The point that counsel for the Prosecution was making is that you are putting to a witness a previous inconsistent statement but you are only putting a part of it because, as she says, later on in the transcript on which you are relying, he explains what he says, so in fairness to the witness and so that it makes sense to the Chamber, you have to put it in its entirety, and that's the second time she's had to make that intervention. So notwithstanding what the witness -- what answer you were able to elicit from the witness today, sometime after the Krajisnik trial the proper context of the question would require you to put the full quotation to the witness. It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept your intervention, of course. I looked at the entire transcript and I also looked -- listened to the audio records. It's been admitted as an exhibit. You are going to listen to it and you are going to find the place where the witness questions his own signature on the document. So this was part of the testimony -- or the record of his testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, you objected to the attendance or lack of attendance at the government sessions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the government adopt a decision that due to frequent sessions and the commitments of the ministers they designate deputies or representatives who would attend these meetings in their absence; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please, please, not the possibility. Is there a government decision on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that we had agreed to do that, and that is the practice. Sometimes if the minister is unable to attend, then a deputy should attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was that logical because of a large number of sessions and the fact that the ministers had to do their job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not a consequence of it being logical because there were too many sessions, but it was a consequence of perhaps too many commitments that the ministers had.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All Right. I'm going to show you the minutes of a government session of the 22nd of July, 1992. This is the 41st session, and it's Exhibit 65 ter 929. Page 2 in the Serbian and perhaps it could be the case that it is also page 2 in the English. Let us just see because in the B/C/S on the second page it's at the end so perhaps let's see if in the English it's also at the bottom of page 2. Well, the B/C/S is good. Now let us find the English, please. Just take it slowly. All right. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you see on the screen one of your ministers, Momcilo Mandic makes the objection that there is no quorum at the meeting, that the number of ministers is not enough for the government to be able to work properly. Mr. Djeric, the minister, about whom you claim was attending irregularly, was the most persistent on insisting that the government should work in its full composition. How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government could not work and its decisions could not be in force unless there was the required number of ministers. This is something that was never done. Please find me a decision that was adopted without a -- all the legal requirements being met.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm saying that the next speaker at the session of the government, Mr. Mico Stanisic remarks and objects because the minister of foreign affairs, Aleksa Buha was not attending the session, so the second minister, about whom you said did not attend regularly, intervened and remarked that another different minister was not attending the government session. How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were not present perhaps they were doing their duties. As minister of foreign affair, perhaps he had some other commitments. I mean, his job was not to spend time at Pale at the Presidency or the government seat. That was not part of his job.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not interpret two or three questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I just want to alert you that you have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't even need more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Stanisic objected because Mr. Aleksa Buha did not attend, and you in turn justify that absence by stating and by telling the government that at a meeting of the Presidency it was agreed that the seat of the foreign ministry is in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president asked him that he worked there, and Buha was very tightly connected to him, so the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was closely connected to the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And let me remind you, earlier in response to my answers -- questions when I asked you why Buha was not good to you, you said that he -- that was because he leaned towards Belgrade too much.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never said that. You interpreted that to mean that he was leaning too much towards Belgrade. I think that is your decision. I never said anything like that. This is a question of your decision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the speakers are going too fast for a proper interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You heard what the interpreters have said. The gap between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Like this, I'm not going to bother you any more about the sessions, the positions. I would like to say something about the work that is expecting us -- that is awaiting us, Your Honours, about these documents. I would like to ask the witness about something.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Permit me, we have another 10 minutes, and I'm not going allow you to even take a second of that time. I'm not even going to grant you one second.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never said that the reason was because he was leaning towards Belgrade. That is your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please be patient. You are taking my seconds from me. The Trial Chamber will weigh your answer. Mr. Djeric, I would like to ask you a principled question. You attended many Assembly sessions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes or no, just say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you, don't be afraid. I'm just asking you whether you did or didn't. Did you listen to the addresses of those deputies who spoke?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was present I did listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you the addresses of deputies Prstojevic, Madam Plavsic, and so on. I'm going to remind you about Mr. Prstojevic, you said in relation to him that you couldn't know what he was thinking when he was stating certain political positions or plans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember putting it quite that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I para-phased. The question was, what do you think Mr. Prstojevic meant when his address was being quoted, so I'm asking you concretely, can you remember that you said that Biljana Plavsic did have a right to her own opinion and that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are para-phrasing again. This is bothering me. I didn't say that she had the right to her own opinion. But what I said was that this is her opinion and she stated that opinion. We are not saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If these things are different that we are saying, then I'm asking you, does every deputy have the right to their own opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Does the constitution guarantee that a deputy can say anything at the podium in the Assembly without replying, does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is parliamentary practice that any deputy can state their own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Deputies, using that right of theirs in exercising their right, did they frequently present some sort of personal promotion or promote their region and then after those addresses of theirs, there was no political action or any kind of parliamentary or Assembly decision as a result of that address; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies freely voiced their opinions. They discussed things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question is, by taking out of context parts of certain addresses, are you able to reach conclusions about the policies of a state or a parliamentary body? Are there any dangers in that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's always a danger in taking things out of context, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Would it be the most proper thing then to take into account only the final product of the Assembly, some law that it adopts or a declaration, a resolution, and to consider them as the basis of some policy being conducted by the Assembly; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The products are the most important things, the outcome. But in any case, part of the policy is also the discussion, all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to talk about the way or the manner of conducting a discussion or a debate. If a third person is making the minutes and then summarises your address in three sentences in the third person, so to say, and that that person chooses what is relevant in summarising that, can you draw conclusions on the basis of such a summary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that should not be the case. You are asking me now something that, you know, I did not have the opportunity to look at the minutes, how they were summarised, how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because all the minutes, there is an Assembly and then there is the summary of government meetings, they were all summarised in the third person, and the summaries were two or three sentences per person. Is this an authentic way of noting down what is said and can it be taken as a authentic substance of the discussion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me something that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you suggesting the Assembly minutes are like that? They are not, they are taped. The government minutes, I agree, but you said the Assembly. Do you mean the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. Well, you didn't understand me. I found also an Assembly session whose minutes were done in a summarised form. This is the 13th Assembly session of the 24th of March. This is 65 ter 291.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry. You were dealing with the Assembly where Mrs. Plavsic and Prstojevic spoke. That was a taped Assembly. Or are you just saying there was one Assembly where there wasn't tapes? That's what is not clear on the transcript, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Madam Korner. I just referred to one matter from the Assembly and the bulk of the example relates to the government meetings where the minutes were taken in summary form of the proceedings, so you are right, the Assembly sessions were taped and then later transcribed, but government sessions were recorded in this form that I'm referring to. I'm saying the whole of this thing in order to see whether we would be able to use this document or this -- these documents as authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you know how the government session meeting minutes were processed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to give you a specific question. Who summarised the discussion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the government secretary. She took minutes. She was responsible for the minutes and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that he is qualified to summarise your, let's say, voluminous discussion or discussion by some other member of the government? Is he fit to properly summarise what was being said and pick the most important things? Can he perhaps fail in this task?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: First part of the witness's answer we did not catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends whether there was a proposal of some discussion or, I don't know exactly what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he can or not, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, they are saying that the first part of your answer was not recorded. Can you please repeat now what you said. If I'm not mistaken, who summarised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes were summarised by the secretary of the government. And he is the person who, according to his job specification and the usual practice was charged with taking minutes of government sessions and he did that in the manner that is presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no more question, I have no more questions, I have no more questions. Just one. Just one. I'm finishing. I'm finishing with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question was, I am afraid that the answer was not recorded, would such a summary of the minutes regardless of his qualifications has the potential danger that he did not accurately summarise the discussion in three sentences that was much longer than that? Is there such a danger?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if somebody deliberately would like to do something, that is always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some minutes were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Djeric. Thank you very much, Your Honours, I have finished with my cross-examination, and I think that some procedural questions about these minutes we can discuss without the witness. As far as I'm concerned, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Pantelic cross-examines. Can I say that the answers to the questions about Mr. Prstojevic and Mrs. Plavsic come in the transcript of the 30th of October 2370. And Mr. Cvijetic's summary is perhaps not very accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for Mr. Pantelic to get prepared, there is one intervention in the transcript. Page 55, row 12. Mr. Cvijetic said 65 ter 2 -- sorry, can I just -- let me just check the other number, Your Honours. Please just bear with me. He said 65 ter 29 -- sorry. We will make a proper objection. I'm sorry, he lost it because I didn't want to interrupt and now I forgot the number. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric. I'm attorney Igor Pantelic, and I am defending Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The best way for us to speed things up is that when I put the question to you, you can look on your screen and when the cursor stops moving then you can begin your answer because then we are also helping the court reporters and the interpreters. I think it's proper to proceed in this way. Mr. Djeric, I formed the impression from your testimony and on the basis of analysis of the documents in this case, that you, in spite of major difficulties in the beginning of the establishment of Republika Srpska, nevertheless worked professionally and diligently when you were prime minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to my work, others can evaluate it, but I did my best to build rule of law and to secure conduct that was in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And with that goal in mind you placed a lot of emphasis on having the Justice Ministry and the Ministry of the Interior do their duties professionally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I considered them to be key ministries without which there would be no government. If those two ministries did not function at the appropriate level, the government would not be a successful one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the Army of Republika Srpska, a member of your government was the minister of defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, of course, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in the professional sense carried out its duties in relation to the organisation of defence of Republika Srpska and in military organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in cooperation with the command of course, meaning the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you and I can agree that the basic principle is that when war operations are underway, the military commander is the main coordinator in all aspects in a specific area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was for the most part. In places where operations were being conducted from what I know everything was subordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in that context, from what I can remember, a meeting was held of the extended War Presidency in June 1992. This is document on 65 ter list 1229. You mentioned that document in response to a question by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Registry to show the document on the screen, please. 65 ter 1229. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At this meeting General Gvero informed, as we can see in paragraph 2 of these minutes, he reported of a certain situation in the area of the Banja Luka corps because it was noted that there were widespread crimes prevalent in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I was just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also in item 11, it was decided to draft instructions to the Serbian Army, Army of Republika Srpska, in relation to the compulsory provisions of the Geneva Conventions; is that correct? Are you able to see paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to look at another document that is related to this one because this document, if I'm not mistaken, is dated the 9th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask the Registry to put on the screen for us our document 2D07-0049, which is in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Probably this copy is not the best, but can you please look at this document. It's dated the 20th of June 1992, and the Main Staff is sending a dispatch and instructions out. Can we please scroll up so that we can see who signed the document and to whom the document was sent. We can see the document was drafted by Milan Gvero, General Gvero, and that it was sent to the command of the 1st, 2nd Krajina Corps and to certain brigades; is that correct, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm unable to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, we are just noting whether that is what it says in this document. I'm not asking you if you know whether this was dispatched or not. I mean, it's in the document, you can see it, right? Now, if we look at paragraph 1 of this document, we can see there that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in paragraph 1 is talking about cases of retribution against -- or reprisals against innocent people such as looting, burning, destruction, and mistreatment. Then it says that such actions damage the reputation and the moral image of the Serbian soldier. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, do we have the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat for the sake of the record?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you see what it says in item 1?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I need time to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, please go ahead, read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While that is happening can I just ask, because we've got two witnesses here at the moment, how long Mr. Pantelic thinks he is going to be. I think we might as well send one away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Re-examination. Yes, it's going to be fairly short.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, for the transcript, Mr. Djeric, in item 1 you've read it, have you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it says that the Main Staff is pointing out that members of the army have to respect certain international norms and not allow retribution against the civilian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that at government level, attention was drawn to the fact that the army needed to prevent such occurrences, the army was told about this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our standpoint in general. As you were able to see, I wrote. But the army as an institution was a problem of the Presidency. The government had no connection to the ministry except for quartermaster affairs, financing and so on. I'm saying this for the simple reason that the idea of government, the concept of government has been transposed to various other institutions, and that's how certain problems arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise, I don't know if this is in e-court. I just have the ERN number. It's 03605772. Let's just see whether we have this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the -- it's 5.20. It's time for the usual break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I assist, Mr. Pantelic. It's 65 ter 2673.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back in I just wanted to alert counsel, they may have heard it already, of the shift on Thursday from the afternoon to the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You are about to show a document to the witness, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. This is, thanks to the intervention of my learned friend Ms. Korner, this is 65 ter document 2673, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, this is a document which is practically an order issued by the government of the 21st of May, 1992. In the preamble, as you see, the session was held on the 21st of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the gist of this order is, if I'm not wrong, in view of the fact that wartime activities are going on, the movements of men liable for military service or conscripts are to be limited, and those who fail to respect this will have measures taken against them by the military organs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may just be my screen, but all I've got in front of me is the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Same here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would be nice to have the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I think we all have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours have it in English, do you? I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'm looking at point 3, item 3 of this order. It came into effect right after it was adopted, and it was sent to the municipal Crisis Staffs, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We may conclude then that the government in cooperation with the appropriate ministry, it was the Ministry of Defence in this case, took all measures to put all available human resources at the service of the defence of the republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was done by the Ministry of Defence which was in charge of mobilisation so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the goal, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like us to see the document which my colleague Mr. Cvijetic discussed -- let me just see what number it is. It's MFI P260.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I have only ERN number. It's 00949847. No, no, it is the other one. 65 ter 1129 [sic]. 65 ter 129. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 229, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 192. Then we have a -- mixing up something. Mr. Cvijetic has a number of 65 ter 192, but obviously it is not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That was the report on paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, paramilitary formation, Your Honour. Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, when answering questions put to you by my colleague Mr. Cvijetic, you looked at this document. As the author of this document, is the security service of the Main Staff, Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, who was the chief, tell me the following: In your contact with Colonel Tolimir, did you see him as a professional, a military professional? Was that your assessment of him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I didn't make any assessments of Tolimir. I didn't have any contacts with him because he was in the military line and had contact with the Presidency. He had nothing to do with me. That was the army. And the president of the republic had relations with the army. I neither assessed him and I -- nor was I involved in any of this. I was very far away from it. The government had no connection at all. It had nothing to do with military cadres apart from mobilisation, the quartermaster service, the budget, financing. That was what the Ministry of Defence dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the armies of Republika Srpska, the Muslim Federation, the HVO consisted of former officers of the JNA for the most part?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were professional officers there, but to what extent they made up the army, I can't say with any precision. It's correct that there were former officers there in the armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that they had gone through rather good military training, we have no reason to doubt that they were professionals in their job, that they knew how do their job; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this report compiled by Colonel Tolimir on behalf of the Main Staff, as it mentions events that you yourself referred to, we have no reason to doubt the authenticity of this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot verify it, I cannot check it, I can only accept it as it stands, but I have no knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. You know that there were paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's another issue. But as for Tolimir and the army, I can't speak about that because simply they had no links to me. As for paramilitary formations, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This document was compiled by the security service of the Army of Republika Srpska, the author is Colonel Tolimir, and it speaks of paramilitary formations. You went through this with my colleague Mr. Cvijetic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I was even asked by one of the Judges, and I can answer his question now, that paramilitary formations were extra-institutional. They emerged at a certain point of time. There were various groups of various strengths, but what was most important certain local authorities and even commercial enterprises or companies from those areas recruited and paid these units. They found them, the members in Serbia and throughout the region, they brought them there to guard their villages, and quite simply, they found men, paid them, and these local authorities often used the budgets of the local companies to pay the wages of these groups. And it was very hard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did they also arm these groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who armed them. I don't know, but I believe that the local authorities and the companies paid for everything, and these groups had their own interests, and later on, it was very difficult to deal with these groups because they got used to having their own interests there. So it was very difficult to eliminate them. They became very deeply routed in these areas, and it was very difficult to get rid of them. It was very difficult to deal with them afterwards. I heard about some of the groups mentioned here and others I've never heard of mentioned here. For example, Suva Rebra I've never heard of them. As for Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Captain Dragan, yes, I have heard of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, sorry, some of the groups apparently were not recruited on a local basis such as, for instance, Seselj's men, I would imagine that they would be recruited through Mr. Seselj's political party. Can you confirm this, that some of the groups were not recruited on any local basis but were recruited throughout Serbia and in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I didn't say that these were local people, but it was the local authorities who found these men in the general area. Most often they were not local people. There may have been some local people who joined them, I don't know. I can't be precise about this, but they were found in the general area and paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, it appears that at least at some point the paramilitary groups were assisting the army in some of the combat operations in that they would perform ancillary duties during and after combat operations. Are you able to provide any information about the relations that existed between the paramilitary groups and the army based on the knowledge or the information that you received as prime minister? What I'm asking you is that since we have seen that apparently the problem of controlling the paramilitaries was brought up at several occasions in meetings not only in the Presidency, but also in the Assembly, so you must have been present at at least some of the occasions where these problems were discussed. And so my first question to you is, from that information that you received during these meetings, did you or were you able to form any opinion about how the army and the paramilitary formations worked together? And, sir, if you don't know then just say so, but please be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I heard that they had problems because in the end the army wanted to get rid of paramilitary formations as well. The government discussed this issue more than once and demanded that these paramilitary formations be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that this was the -- I understand that this was the position of the -- of your government, that they should be prevented from taking any part in the armed conflicts as such. But what was the position in the Presidency and in the Assembly? Are you able to tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, they approved of that. There were different views here held by the government and the Presidency. The Presidency approved, as you were able to see from what Mrs. Plavsic said in the discussion. She thought they were fighters and so on and so forth. But the problem of these military units and armies, it was more within the competency of the Presidency. We dealt with the paramilitary formations insofar as they were obstructing normal life and the normal order of things, and we asked that they be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me when I say that both the government and the Assembly and the Army of Republika Srpska issued several decisions to put the paramilitary formations under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now that we are looking at this document, let's look at page 5 of the Serbian version, and that's page 4 of the English version. In paragraph 2, you see that this is about a paramilitary formation called SOS from Banja Luka; is that right? Have you read this part?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's the second line from the top. The text begins "the Serbian defence forces, SOS..." read just that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do we see here? We see that this paramilitary group, SOS, was under the command of a man called Nenad Stevandic, and he was also the president of the Serbian Sokol society; is that right? Do you happen to know whether this is an association of people raising hawks, or do you know what this society is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a sports society. A sports association. It existed in the time of the first Yugoslavia, the one that lasted from 1918 to 1941. I don't know what this society dealt with specifically. It was called the falcon, the falcon society, Sokol, falcon, but here the name reads slightly differently, it's not Sokol, it's Sokolsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now an experienced intelligence man, Colonel Tolimir says in his document that some private businessmen have a considerable influence over this SOS group, leaders from the public security station in Banja Luka as well. That's what it says here, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: SJB is short for the local police station, public security station; is that right? Do you know that this is the abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you tell me, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What, you are not a policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a policeman, I didn't work in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But it's quite simple, Mr. Djeric, it's a question of etymology. Just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you tell me it's an abbreviation, I have no reason to say it's not. You are just helping me to find my way in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. So SJB is a local police station, is it not? It refers to any local police station; is that right? For the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've already agreed to that. You have translated these abbreviations to me, and I accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: SNB is the service of national security, so before 1992, this was the state security, the DB, but then from 1992 there was a change in the law so now that indicates the service of national security, SNB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the experienced Colonel Tolimir goes on to say that a number of criminals had infiltrated that group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I'm seeing this for the first time so all I can do is note what I'm seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. But you know that in many such groups, there were many criminals and persons of a dubious morality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, like I said, that person was a businessman and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now the document goes on and it said that a part of that unit was incorporated into that formation of the Special Police detachment of the CSB but is not under the actual command of the detachment or the CSB. That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, it says that a part of those -- that group of criminals headed by a certain Branko Palackovic is investigative jail, so something was done by the police to place these people under control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the last page of this document. That is page 6 in the Serbian, and it's page 6 too in the English version. And what we can see is that the dispatch was received on the 13th of August 1992 at the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the conclusion in the document, which was drafted by the VRS Main Staff, is that every armed Serb in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina must be under the single command of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if not, would need to be disarmed and subject to the provisions of the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I assume that you have some information that the army did take certain measures and that once the military Prosecution and military courts were formed, such crimes were prosecuted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could see that here and that -- that's what they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Djeric, I have no more questions for you, Professor Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I want to go back over a few matters that you were asked about in the last few days. First of all, you told Mr. Cvijetic yesterday when you were being shown a document about the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka about a number of regions being cut off. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Krajina region, the Herzegovina region, so on and so forth. For how long do you say these regions were cut off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krajina was cut off until the units managed to break through, until the corridor was formed. The corridor of life, as they called it. But even then the corridor was not safe, it wasn't safe for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough date, before I put a date to you, when the corridor was opened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to. I think that it was in the summer, but simply it wasn't in my domain, so I really don't -- I mean, it was a matter for the army -- army, actions I'm unable to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you've asserted that these areas were cut off, and I'm just going to see if you can assist. Would the middle of July sound about right, when the corridor was opened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was summer when the corridor was opened, but it did remain unsafe for a few months after that, but I think it was summer when the corridor was opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but we've looked at the minutes of the Assembly meeting of the 24th of July, and a number of people were able to attend from the Banja Luka area, weren't they, Mr. Djeric? Including Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it can't have been that cut off by July, can it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, until the corridor -- or before the corridor was established, it was not possible to pass. We were unable to pass. It's another matter if the army was able to get through by helicopters or some other ways. I mean, regular people were unable to and we were not able to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, sorry, Mr. Djeric. The Trial Chamber is going to hear some evidence in any event about the corridor operations, but do you accept -- do you agree you've seen the minutes, that Mr. Kupresanin was at the meeting of the 24th of July? Just get the right date actually. Yes, between the 24th and the 26th of July. Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that report. You are mentioning Kupresanin. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We looked at the minutes of the -- and you can have them up again on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 65 ter 928, please. English it's page 40, and in the B/C/S it's page 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kupresanin come from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is -- he comes from Banja Luka, so he should have come from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I have it on my screen now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the gentleman below whose name I always have terrible difficulty with, Cancar -- Cancar? Did he come from Foca?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just please tell me where this Assembly session was being held? I'm not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This Assembly session I can tell you, was held, I believe, in Pale. I can confirm that in a minute. Sorry, just give me one moment, and I can tell you where it was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think the meeting on 24th to 26th July was held in Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jahorina. Jahorina. Thank you. Much the same thing I think to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, I don't want to spend too much time on this, Mr. Djeric. By July, it does appear, doesn't it, that areas which had at some stage or another been cut off, had not -- were no longer cut off? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do in principle accept that. As of the end of July definitely it was possible to pass. I don't know what the security status of the roads was though. I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next I want to -- you were shown a document which was 65 ter 606 which was the Sanski Most Crisis Staff decision apparently appointing Mr. Vrucinic. I don't want to have that up again, but could we look at, please -- perhaps I can just ask you to deal with that without the document. Were you aware that Mr. Zupljanin had in fact confirmed the appointment of Mr. Vrucinic? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next I want you to have up again, please, 65 ter 176. You were asked about that yesterday at LiveNote 24 -- page 2459. And it's page 3 of the English version, I think. Paragraph -- is this the right one? Never mind that. I won't bother to ask you anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you were asked a number of questions about the TAS Volkswagon saga. Now, you were shown a document, first of all -- I hope this is the right number, 1398.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Yes. I'm very sorry, there's volumes of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Here. This was the report of the inspectors to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page in the English and presumably the second page in the B/C/S, because it's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I can't remember whether you said you ever saw this report, I don't think you did. But do you see in the middle of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For some reason you were shown this report. But in the middle of the last paragraph do you see: "In addition, Borislav Maksimovic stated that almost every one of his police employees had stolen a Golf which can be seen, but they would return them if anyone ever asked them to do so." Now, were you aware that Mr. Maksimovic, who was in fact the chief of the SJB, was saying that all of his employees had stolen the Golfs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, and I didn't say. You mentioned me saying something. I didn't say anything. I'm seeing these documents for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. You were shown this yesterday, so I thought I'd ask you about that. Did Mico Stanisic ever report to you that his inspectors were reporting to him that members of the police force were stealing these Golfs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no. It was, among other things, one of the key points in the context of this entire problem that we were discussing, the TAS factory, the Golf cars. I mean, that was a problematic issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just correct line 15. I said, did Mico Stanisic ever report to you that his inspectors were reporting to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look at a couple of other documents about this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up on the screen, please, 65 ter 3094. That last report was the 12th of July. There's no English. Why is there no English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, while we are looking for the document, did you ever know about how many stolen Golfs this was about? How many cars were involved? Because I'm a little bit surprised that this is something the government was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll see a reason why in a minute. If I can get this -- I don't know why we only seem to have the B/C/S, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have I got the right -- is this -- yes, 16th of July. For some unknown reason, although I seemed to have managed to download the English version last night, it doesn't appear ... Sorry. All right, I can move on to a further document and come back to this one. Can we try 65 ter 318.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This again is the CSB from Romanija Birac reporting on the 27th of August, 1992 about the Vlasenica SJB. Talking again about vehicles. And saying: "So far 23 vehicles have been confiscated which five have been returned after checks. They stress there are big problems as a result of constant requests from the political leadership and the Republika Srpska MUP that vehicles be returned to certain persons without any checks, and there have even been occasions when requests have been made for the return of the vehicles that were being driven with obviously false documents." Now, this relates to the political leadership and the MUP. Were you aware of the -- anybody -- firstly, did you ever deal with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It talks about the political leadership ordering vehicles to be returned. Did you ever make such request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would sometimes write to the army asking them to check if these cars were being used to simply exclude them from the traffic. I remember writing an order to the army to put a stop to these things. To the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't follow that answer at all. What this note is saying is that they have been, the SJB in Vlasenica has been confiscating cars, there's not proper documentation. They say there's been an interference from the political leadership and the Republika Srpska MUP asking that vehicles be returned to persons without any checks. And I didn't quite understand your answer. Did you ever write, not to the army, but to the police, saying they should return vehicles to people who had been stopped?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall writing, but it was asked of the Ministry of the Interior to be active in that respect. I don't recall, although, I did make efforts to put this under control, to prevent these thefts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still don't understand your answer, Mr. Djeric, but I think it's getting late so I'll move on. Can I now come back to the document --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question so that's why it's hard for me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The police here -- I'll try one more time. The police here are complaining there is political interference in their work from people who are in the leadership, who when they stop people and take away cars because they don't have proper papers, someone in the leadership orders the police in Vlasenica to return them. And I'm asking whether you ever interfered to this extent? Now do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not interfere. I never intervened in that respect. Everything I did was quite simply to put a stop to this kind of behaviour. But I did it through the Ministry of the Interior or through the army to have this prevented. It wasn't me. But probably there were such things in the highest leadership because how would the convoys be able to pass through had not that been there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the document I was trying to ask you about because we do now have it. We have it in sanction, not in e-court. It's 65 ter 3094.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a note, again, by the CSB in Romanija Birac dated the 16th of July, 1992. And again we are still referring to this question of the TAS motor cars. In the second paragraph there's an interview with Mr. Maksimovic, again a second interview. Then we see that in later on six of the Golf vehicles were registered for the needs of Vogosca, and then Mr. Koprivica and Nikola Poplasen, who you said you knew, is that right, you knew who these people were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Poplasen was an university Professor, and I knew him as an assistant professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. "...a government commissioner gave us information on how vehicles from the factory had been put at the disposal of various organs and institutions." And at the bottom of that paragraph does it say this, Mr. Koprivica also said that before the war Presidency passed a decision that is to say for the vehicles, he ordered that six Golf vehicles be given for the needs of the government of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the vehicles were sent directly to the prime minister. Now, that's you Mr. Djeric. Did you get those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government made official orders and these were paid for. Everything that the government ordered, it paid for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terrible sorry, I didn't want to interrupt, but this document in fact doesn't say, this in Serbian. I didn't have time to check the English translation, but this one talks about the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 1 it talks about the Presidency, but the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The best thing would be if the witness reads out the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph. We are on the wrong page, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I withdraw. I haven't seen this part. I was watching the first page. I'm sorry. It's probably the time and everybody is tired. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does say prime minister there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It does, it does, it does.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about reading it out, Mr. Djeric. So what this is saying is that vehicles have been taken from the TAS factory and supplied to the government and that you had got them all, and you're saying, yes, you did get them all but you paid for them; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the government ordered goods, it paid for them. The government certainly paid what it received. The problem here is theft, so these things are being mixed up here. The government asked for vehicles because it needed them, but it paid for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when you ordered and paid for the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but the vehicles were paid for immediately. Immediately. Delivery could not be taken without evidence that the payment had been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but what was happening here apparently, as you know, was there was whole scale theft of motor vehicles from this factory by police officers and everybody else as far as one can tell. That's what the scandal was, wasn't it, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The government is only mentioned here because some vehicles that had been on stock had been delivered to the government, so somebody stood there and didn't let the vehicles leave without certain documents. A lot of things are being mixed up here. The problem here is vehicles being stolen, vehicles not being paid for. And how this was possible? How was it possible for this to be done in the face of the minister -- Ministry of Interior and the factory services and other services? How can cars leave the factory without somebody checking what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move then to another topic. You were asked for some reason to look at documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I ask. Mr. Djeric, do you know how many cars were involved? How many cars were stolen more or less? 10, 50, 100, more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are thousands of cars at issue. I don't know the precise number, but this factory was a very rich one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the first document Ms. Korner showed you a few minutes ago, it was said 2300; would you agree to that? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I know that -- well, I can't say how many precisely, but I know that the company had considerable amounts of goods on stock. It was a well to do factory, and that's why the problem was so huge. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, just for the record, I see that your answer is not on the record when I asked you 2300, would you agree more or less to that figure. What was your answer to that? So in the document they said 2300. Was that more or less the figure you were thinking about? You said thousands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said some thousands, 1- or 2.000. I'm just speaking in general terms. All I know is that there were considerable stocks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just two other matters, please, or three really. For some reason you were asked to look at documents relating to the arrest of men connected with the Mice and you were also asked about the Yellow Wasps. Do you know what happened to the people who were arrested from the Mice and the Yellow Wasps? And if you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were also shown a letter written to you by Stanisic on the 18th of July of 1992, and it was put to you that it was Mico Stanisic who was the person who originated the idea that there should be an investigation into war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look very quickly please at 65 ter 1180. And can we go, please, to the third page in English and the third page in B/C/S. I think you may have looked at this document already. These are government -- just a minute, what was that date? 65 ter 1183? No, no, no, no. I should a have said 118 -- it's my own note, yes. Just a minute, let me check. Yes, sorry, it's my mistake, 1183, please, third page in English, third page in B/C/S. Should be the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the 3rd of June, a month and a half or nearly two months before Mr. Stanisic writes that letter. Do we see that at the session of the government a procedure -- it's discussed that a procedure for determining war crimes should be initiated responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior and the Committee for War Crimes formed by the government. Do you know whose idea it was that this --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the government's idea. The Commission for War Crimes, you see, is something the government had been working on for a long time. It established this commission, and it was decided that all perpetrators should be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Cvijetic put to you that the essence of your objection to Mico Stanisic and Momcilo Mandic was that they were closer to the president than to you. That was at page 29 today. And he interrupted your answer. Can you tell us now finally what your objection was to both Mico Stanisic and Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply this intervention by counsel does not hold water. I didn't have problems with them because they were the president's men, but simply because I was not satisfied with their work because these were two key ministries in implementing certain government decisions, especially those government decisions concerning security of property, security of persons, and so on, and all decisions of that nature. And that is why I had certain problems with them. Because we concluded that all perpetrators of crimes should be prosecuted and who can do that on behalf of the government but the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice. These were the two ministries that were supposed to implement the government decisions. But they were ignoring the government. They kept visiting the president, or going out to the field. They didn't attend one session after another. Sessions were held in their absence. So quite simply they felt, well, that the government could be pushed aside. They thought of themselves as belonging to the top leadership and that was the problem because the government was unable to do its work in those areas. We didn't have basic information, the necessary coordination was not in place, you know. There are some jobs falling within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior that can be done by clerks and civil servants but there are things that cannot be done without the minister. So there was lack of information, lack of coordination. And if you insisted on that, you would come up against resistance or you would be ignored because in a one-party regime things like this happen. And they did happen. It wasn't that I had a certain attitude towards them because they were the president's men. Of course they were the president's men. No president would allow a minister of justice or a minister of the interior not to be his man. I didn't mind that. What I minded was that not enough work was being done on implementing the government programme, and implementing government decisions, especially as regards these matters that I've mentioned. You see, it's a crime when you fail to prosecute crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, did you ever raise this with Mico Stanisic before you complained at the meeting at the end of November, the Assembly at the end of November? Did you ever raise this with Mico Stanisic personally, that in your view he was not doing the job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my practice with Minister Stanisic and other ministers. First, I would speak to them, you know. I always tried to correct things, clarify things, point out problems, and only then would I turn to the government and after that to the political leadership, and after that to the Assembly. When I saw that nothing could be done and that it was reflecting on the government, because when the other ministers saw that you were unable to get anything done, then they too simply gave up, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was his reaction --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gave up on you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was his reaction when you raised it with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He… simply protested, he believed that was not the case. He was generally impertinent, impertinent, and he wasn't in favour of a dialogue, of an agreement. You know, he was a man who sort of… liked a bit to play the role of a powerful man surrounded by five or six escorts in full armour and so on... He even told me once that he would cool me down, and what can you…

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I have one question. Yesterday you said about crimes, and especially robbery and looting, you've said and I read the transcript: "This was quite prominent for the reason that the crime which was rampant was undermining the authority of the government, especially if ministers or parts of the state administration were actually taking part in such activities." Can you explain what you meant by that? Ministers or parts of the state administration that are actually taking part in such activities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this has not been noted down properly because I was talking about crime and that it was not a good thing when ministers participated in crime because it then affected the functioning of government, but I was speaking in another context when I said that we took measures to prosecute all those who are violating the law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you say now that ministers take part in crime. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information reached me to the effect that crime was made possible primarily by the participation of these two ministers in those crimes. Minister Stanisic and Minister Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric, you are now released as a witness. You may return to your home, and we wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the last statement -- I will -- the last statement made by the witness I think gives the Defence a right to -- the right to cross-examine him on this, on the statement he has just made. Otherwise it will remain unclarified what sort of crime he is referring to and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I regret that I would have spoken prematurely. You heard Mr. Cvijetic's comment, and it's something that we would have to pursue tomorrow morning. So the cautions, the usual cautions continue and we -- tomorrow afternoon, I'm sorry, I notice the look of alarm on the Registry's face. Tomorrow afternoon. So tomorrow afternoon in this Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of November, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.
